newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Dispute over Bosnia town left unresolved.
newsitem.headline: Dispute over Bosnia town left unresolved.

text.p: A dispute over who should control the pivotal river port town of Brcko still casts a shadow over the process of building peace in Bosnia after three years of war.
A U.S. arbiter concluded it was better to avoid a clear resolution of the issue for another year than risk reigniting a war over who should control the northern town.
Washington's envoy to the Balkans, John Kornblum, called the arbiter's ruling on Friday "definitely enough" to prevent renewed fighting between Bosnian Serb and Moslem forces.
It allows Bosnian Serbs, a pre-war minority in Brcko, to remain in control until 1998 when the issue will be revisited.

Returning Brcko to Moslem-Croat control would have isolated the Bosnian Serb pocket in northwest Bosnia, including the industrial town of Banja Luka, from the bulk of Bosnian Serb territory in the east.
In the meantime, an "international supervisor" is supposed to oversee the return of Moslem and Croat refugees to their Brcko homes and promote economic reconstruction.
But the ruling gave no clear executive authority to the supervisor and did not set out a mechanism to punish either faction for violating the arbiter's decision.

Carl Bildt, the international High Representative to Bosnia, whose office will appoint the supervisor for Brcko, warned reporters over the weekend that there were "no guarantees" that Serb authorities would comply.
"It is sometimes easier to write a thing in a Washington law firm than to do it on the ground in Brcko," he said.
Bosnian Moslem leaders and political analysts say the key to defusing tensions over Brcko is to allow refugees expelled from the town early in the 1992-95 war to return.
But ultra-nationalist Serb authorities have repeatedly refused to allow Moslem or Croat refugees to move back to territory which now lies inside Bosnia's Serb entity.
In a year from now, the United States and European powers could be facing the same conundrum over Brcko, possibly aggravated by a local election.

As Bosnian Moslems rebuild their army with the help of a U.S.-sponsored military aid programme, Serb authorities are ironically counting on the long-term deployment of NATO troops to prevent any possible Moslem offensive.

Bosnian Serb leaders once had their army fire on and capture soldiers in the U.N. peacekeeping force. Now they are grateful for the presence of the NATO-led peace force, which has U.S. troops patrolling Brcko.

The 18-month mandate for the NATO force expires in mid-1998. But diplomats have already predicted NATO will stay in Bosnia beyond 1998 to maintain the peace and head off another influx of refugees heading to Western Europe.
The Bosnian Serbs, who conquered Brcko in 1992, say privately they are confident that the peacekeeping force will remain in Bosnia indefinitely.
"NATO's never going to leave. This place will become some sort of Cyprus," said one Serb official, who asked not to be named.
Analysts say the Bosnian Moslems are closing the military gap with the Serbs, who enjoyed a big advantage in heavy weaponry during the war.

The International Crisis Group, a London-based private agency monitoring the peace process, says NATO could be stuck in Bosnia indefinitely unless major powers lean on Serb authorities to allow Brcko refugees to move back.
"If we don't see any return of refugees, then you get to the stage in which the only way to get home is to fight," Chris Bennett, an analyst with ICG, told Reuters.
